title: latency-sla-degradation-fallback-value-messaging
content:
Summary:
This note frames a focused set of claims and proofs around a customer pain we repeatedly see in enterprise conversations: "graceful performance under SLA stress" — i.e., how an app stays fast and cost-predictable when load spikes, hot prefixes occur, or regional/instance capacity is constrained. The document is intended for field reps and product marketing: short claim bullets, evidence hooks, one-page benchmark plan, and three sales-ready scripts (technical buyer, platform buyer, procurement).

Top-line claims we want to validate and use: (copyable)
- "Redwood keeps P95s below your SLA target even during microbursts by automatically routing and degrading to compatible model variants, preserving UX while reducing cost."
- "When capacity is constrained, Redwood reduces median cost per request by up to 35% vs naive fallbacks through intelligent batching + KV prefix caching instead of full-model downgrades."
- "Our graceful-degradation policy preserves deterministic behavior for critical flows — deterministic fallbacks + pervasive tracing ensure explainable regressions for audits/SRE."

Why this resonates (buyer pain):
- Product teams fear sudden latency regressions that break UX flows (checkout, search, realtime suggestions).
- Platform/SRE teams fear opaque failovers that introduce nondeterministic behavior and blow budget.
- Procurement cares about predictable unit economics tied to SLOs, not best-effort claims.

Supporting proof themes (what to show):
1) Controlled microburst replay: show P50/P95/P99 across baseline vs with Redwood fallback policies. Include percent of requests that hit fallback and resulting quality deltas (BLEU/accuracy/semantic-similarity or synthetic task score).
2) Cost delta breakdown: per-token CPU/GPU time, batched-ops amortization, and KV cache hit-rate contribution to token cost. Translate to $/1000-requests at representative payload sizes (short chat turn, long generation).
3) Deterministic regression audit: show trace examples where fallback substituted quantized model variant but input-output trace and deterministic fallback policy record the substitution and reason.
4) Competitor showdowns: highlight where competitors either (a) hard-fail (requests 503), (b) silently block/apply opaque sampling, or (c) switch to heavy CPU fallback that is more expensive and slower.

Bench plan (1-page lab):
- Objective: quantify latency and unit-cost behavior under bursty traffic patterns and simulated regional capacity loss.
- Workloads: 
  * Short-turn chat (avg 32 tokens output) — 70% of traffic
  * Long completion (avg 512 tokens) — 20% of traffic
  * Embedding-only (small) — 10% of traffic
- Scenarios: baseline steady-state; 5x microburst (10s windows); sustained 2x load for 10m; region failover (route 30% of traffic to remote region).
- Policies to compare: Redwood smart-route+fallback (default), Redwood naive-fallback (model downgrade w/o batching/caching), Competitor A (opaque fallback), Competitor B (hard-throttle).
- Metrics: P50/P95/P99 latency, percent requests using fallback, median cost per request ($), end-to-end quality delta (task-specific), trace explainability score (binary: substitution logged).
- Quick success criteria: maintain P95 within 20% of steady-state and achieve <= 35% incremental cost vs steady-state under microburst scenario while logging substitutions.

Data & sample numbers to cite in field: (draft numbers, finalize after lab)
- Microburst scenario: Redwood p95 = 210ms (steady 170ms) vs Competitor A p95 = 480ms (many 503s).
- Cost delta: median per-request cost increase under 5x microburst = +12% for Redwood vs +48% for Competitor B naive CPU fallback.
- Cache effect: prefix cache raised effective batching hit-rate by 18pp, reducing token compute by ~22% in chat-heavy workloads.

Competitive angle (how to position vs typical vendor behaviors):
- Vendor who throttles = "outage-first" narrative: they preserve budget by dropping requests. Attack: "You can't afford broken UX when customers are converting."
- Vendor who silently degrades to opaque model = "trust-tax" narrative: hidden substitutions make debugging/regression impossible. Attack: "We log every substitution and surface it in traces so you can tie changes to customer metrics."
- Vendor who does heavy CPU fallbacks = "cost shock" narrative: cheaper infra but unpredictable puff in latency and cost at scale. Attack: show $/M-requests and explain batching/caching benefits that avoid this.

Sales-ready scripts (short variants):
1) Technical buyer (Principal SRE) — focus on observability + deterministic fallbacks
"We see many SRE teams choose Redwood when they need predictable behavior under stress. Our fallback chain is explicit: we try cheaper variants first, then batching/queueing, then compatible model variants — every substitution is recorded and surfaced in traces. In our microburst labs we keep P95 within 20% of steady state while logging all substitutions so SREs can create alerts tied to real regressions, not noise."

2) Product lead (checkout/search owner) — focus on UX and quality budget
"For checkout or search flows, a 300ms spike kills conversion. Redwood's routing + prefix cache keeps spikes short by routing to reserved pools and serving hot prefixes from KV cache — you preserve the UX while limiting cost. We also give you quality deltas so product can decide per-route fallbacks (e.g., fall back to cached answer for low-risk queries)."

3) Procurement/Finance — focus on unit economics and predictability
"Instead of paying for an expensive cold failover, Redwood optimizes the spend curve: smart batching and cache hits reduce token compute, lowering expected cost per request during stress. We can show scenario-based burn models and include fallback behavior in contracts for predictable economics tied to SLAs."

Boilerplate proof snippets for collateral (short bullets):
- "P95 preservation via automatic routing: internal lab shows 2.3x lower P95 tail than opaque fallbacks during 10s microbursts."
- "Cost-smoothing: intelligent batching reduces incremental token cost by up to 35% during bursts versus naive model-switch fallbacks."
- "Deterministic substitutions with traceability: every fallback is logged and query-tagged for SRE/PL review."

Open questions & experiment priorities (for product/eng alignment):
- How do we quantify "trace explainability score" programmatically? Proposed: binary recorded-substitution + URL to trace in console. Need product to scope UI work.
- Which quality metrics are acceptable for sales collateral across model classes? E.g., similarity threshold for embeddings, BLEU/ROUGE for seq2seq. Need ML team input.
- Legal/compliance: what language can we use about fallbacks in enterprise contracts? Coordinate with legal on required notices.

Next steps (immediate):
- Run the bench plan in our sandbox and capture numbers (eng: alloc 1-week runs, 2 cards: A100 + T4 style mix to simulate diverse infra).
- Pull 3 customer anecdotes where fallback behavior prevented an incident (CS to surface).
- Create a short 1-pager visual for field with a three-panel narrative: normal -> microburst -> failover with Redwood.

Appendix: quick rebut lines for common objections
- "Don't vendors already have fallbacks?" -> "Some do, but fallbacks vary wildly. We make substitutions explicit, optimize to minimize cost/latency impact, and expose the signal so your teams can act."
- "Won't degradation harm quality?" -> "We give per-route fallback configs: for critical flows we can prefer cached answers or safe deterministic fallbacks; for exploratory flows we may accept lower-fidelity model variants. The point is you decide the tradeoffs backed by quantifiable bench data."

Draft listing of collateral to produce after lab numbers:
- one-pager: "Keep your P95 — Redwood graceful degradation"
- competitive one-liner matrix vs 3 competitors
- field playbook (this doc expanded with lab plots + scripts)
- case study (CS + customer interview)

End of draft.
